source.title: Understanding Memorization from the Perspective of Optimization via Efficient Influence Estimation
source.authors: Fu-Tong Liu; Tao Lin; Martin Jaggi

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied, including appendices; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests learning dynamics under label corruption using subset training and accuracy tracking, rather than directly reproducing the original fitting and test-error measurements.
record.gate_note: The authors cite prior results on random-label fitting and regularization; those cited results are not rows. The paper's own label-corruption dynamics and its stated failure to fit when all labels are random are included. Figure-only trends are not assigned numeric values.
record.test_reason: The study directly refines V6 using corrupted-label learning dynamics and reports a schedule-dependent failure to fit completely random labels, bearing on V1, V2 and V4. Its corruption sweep also tests V2's slowdown component.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is accurate about simultaneous learning and training-procedure dependence, but omits a principal conclusion: on correctly labeled real data, difficult examples contain information useful for easy examples, and memorizing them may improve generalization. The authors emphasize concurrent optimization with faster learning of easy examples, rather than denying the observed speed difference between real and random labels.
record.recipe_differences: Uses turn-over dropout to estimate memorization scores and partitions examples by difficulty, then compares learning dynamics; does not directly reproduce the original full random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that memorization capability depends on the training procedure; with VGG-11 on CIFAR-10, the multi-step learning-rate decay schedule is associated with failure to fit when all labels are random. MNIST Figure 3 uses learning rate 0.01 for clarity, whereas the general MNIST setup uses 0.06.

fits_no_version.finding: On uncorrupted datasets, easy and difficult correctly labeled examples improve simultaneously, with easy examples improving faster; the removed-subset control addresses whether difficult-example gains arise from easy-example learning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Correctly labeled examples of different difficulty are learned concurrently at different speeds.

fits_no_version.finding: Training on difficult correctly labeled examples transfers substantially to easy examples, whereas training on easy examples transfers little to difficult examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transfer between correctly labeled easy and difficult subsets is asymmetric.

record.peer_reviewed: OPT2021: 13th Annual Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning
record.problems: Most dynamics are shown in figures and described qualitatively, with no numerical accuracy values or uncertainty estimates in the text. The all-random-label failure is tied to a particular CIFAR-10 VGG-11 training schedule.

untested.parts: Chance-level test error and successful near-zero training error for completely random labels are not established; the reported all-random result is a fitting failure under one schedule.
No numerical ratio establishes that random-label fitting takes only a small constant factor longer than true-label fitting.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiments.

The supplied text does not establish steadily increasing final test error toward chance across corruption fractions or numerical zero training error at every intermediate fraction. Temporal test-accuracy peaks do not test the cross-fraction prediction.
No controlled tests of weight decay, dropout or augmentation preventing random-label fitting, or of removing regularization on true-label generalization.

missing.what: Add the gradient evidence complementing the accuracy-based V6 result: difficult random-label examples have higher average projected contributions to SGD updates throughout training, while real-label examples have higher within-group gradient cosine similarity. These measures support the authors' optimization interpretation but do not alone establish label fitting.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains figure captions and qualitative descriptions but no readable plotted values. No accuracies, corruption levels beyond those stated, or training-time ratios can be reconstructed. A test-accuracy decline over training is not a contradiction of V4's prediction across corruption fractions.

versions.untested_parts: The paper discusses fitting random labels but does not report an explicit zero or near-zero training-error result with test error at chance for completely random labels under unchanged settings.
Does not report a numerical constant-factor training-time comparison between true and random labels.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments are reported.
The paper does not establish perfect training fit at every corruption level or report that test error rises steadily; it describes a peak and subsequent drop in test accuracy when noise exists.
No experiments testing weight decay, dropout or augmentation as regularizers against random-label fitting or true-label generalization.

The study tracks easy and difficult subsets, including random-label examples, and reports simultaneous learning with different speeds; it does not test the specific causal formulation that shared real-data patterns are learned before noisy labels.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with 20,000 training labels replaced by random labels; tracked full set and real-label and random-label subsets.
rows.value: Easy examples are learnt much faster than difficult ones; small improvement on the difficult subset at initial epochs indicates simultaneous learning.
rows.note: The text describes the dynamics but does not provide numeric accuracies or epochs for fitting.
rows.check: Real-label examples are fitted much faster, but random-label examples already improve during initial epochs, qualifying a strictly sequential interpretation. Subset learning speeds at one corruption level do not establish V2's whole-dataset training-time comparison or V4's corruption-fraction trend.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, Figure 3(a) and accompanying text; Appendix A.

rows.subject: one-hidden-layer MLP
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with 20,000 training labels replaced by random labels; evaluated test accuracy over training.
rows.value: Test accuracy reaches the peak at around 20th epoch, when real data are successfully fitted but random noise is barely fitted; it then drops as random-data training accuracy improves.
rows.note: The accompanying text describes the trajectory; no test-accuracy numbers are stated.
rows.check: Around epoch 20, real data are successfully fitted while random labels are barely fitted, supporting V6's relative learning order. Test accuracy changing over epochs at one corruption level does not measure V4's test-error trend across corruption fractions or V2's training-time comparison.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, paragraph preceding Figure 3; Figure 3(b); Appendix A.

rows.subject: VGG-11
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with different extents of random-label corruption; tracked loss and training and test accuracy.

conditions.value: different extents; exact values not stated in text

rows.measure: Training and test dynamics across corruption levels
rows.value: Difficult instances make learning slower; more difficult examples take longer to fully fit. With noise, test accuracy first peaks, then drops and converges.
rows.locator: Appendix E, Figure 10 and accompanying text
rows.note: The text reports qualitative trends. It does not state exact accuracy values or assert perfect fit at each corruption level.
rows.check: Appendix E explicitly reports slower fitting with more corruption and describes eventual full fitting, subject to the all-random exception in R4. This supports the measured slowdown and fitting components; it does not establish a small constant time factor or steadily worsening final test error across fractions. Aggregate curves do not separately establish V6's real-versus-noisy learning order.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix E, first numbered observation and Figure 10.

rows.subject: VGG-11
rows.operation_detail: Trained on CIFAR-10 with all training labels replaced by random noise under the stated multi-step learning-rate decay schedule.

conditions.value: multi-step learning-rate decay instead of cosine annealing

rows.measure: Ability to fit the training dataset
rows.value: The model becomes incompetent to fit the dataset when all labels are replaced by random noise.
rows.note: This is an explicit textual report of failure to fit under the stated training procedure.
rows.check: The caption explicitly reports failure to fit all-random labels under multi-step learning-rate decay. Specify the tested 200-epoch procedure, initial learning rate 0.01, momentum 0.9 and tenfold decays at epochs 100 and 150. This is a conditional failure, not evidence that VGG-11 cannot memorize under other schedules.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 10 caption; Appendix A specifies the 200-epoch training procedure.

rows.subject: MLP and VGG-11
rows.size_stated: MLP: 4096 hidden neurons; VGG-11 size not stated
rows.operation_detail: Tracked easy and difficult subsets during training and validation on real datasets.

conditions.value: easy and difficult subsets based on memorization scores

rows.measure: Training and test accuracy dynamics on subsets
rows.value: Easy and difficult examples are learnt simultaneously, with easy examples fitted faster; on test data, easy examples reach higher accuracy.
rows.note: Qualitative text supports the reported learning-order result; no numeric curves transcribed.
rows.check: These are uncorrupted real datasets partitioned by memorization score. Difficult correctly labeled examples are not noisy or random labels, so their learning order does not directly test V6.

rows.subject: VGG-11
rows.operation_detail: Trained on MNIST with the difficult subset removed as a control for learning on the remaining training data.
rows.baseline: training with full training data including difficult subset; value not stated
rows.value: Dotted-line control is reported as confirming that difficult-subset training-accuracy improvement is not a side effect of patterns learnt from easy examples.
rows.locator: Section 3.3, Figure 5(a,b) caption and accompanying text
rows.note: The paper says the control confirms this interpretation but gives no numeric values. Subject/model attribution to the control is ambiguous in the supplied text; Figure 5(a,b) covers MNIST with MLP.
rows.check: Correct the subject to the MNIST MLP: Figure 5(a,b) identifies this model. The prose refers to VGG-11 ambiguously. The control concerns difficult correctly labeled examples, not V6's noisy-label learning order.

rows.subject: VGG-11
rows.operation_detail: Trained on an easy subset of CIFAR-10; evaluated accuracy on easy and difficult subsets.
rows.measure: Training accuracy on the two subsets
rows.value: Fast convergence on the easy subset and marginal improvement on the difficult subset.
rows.note: The result is described qualitatively, without numeric values.
rows.check: This measures transfer between correctly labeled easy and difficult subsets, not learning real labels before noisy labels. Accuracy on the difficult subset is validation accuracy because that subset is excluded from training.

rows.subject: VGG-11
rows.operation_detail: Trained on a difficult subset of CIFAR-10; evaluated accuracy on easy and difficult subsets.
rows.measure: Training accuracy on the two subsets
rows.value: Despite relatively slow convergence on the difficult subset, training benefits both the difficult and easy subsets substantially.
rows.note: The result is described qualitatively, without numeric values.
rows.check: This measures transfer between correctly labeled subsets rather than V6. Accuracy on the easy subset is validation accuracy because only the difficult subset is used for training.
